subject: biology
source: Podstawa programowa kształcenia ogólnego dla liceum i technikum, biologia, zakres podstawowy (Dz.U. 2018 poz. 467), działy I–IV i cele ogólne III; treści spoza zakresu podstawowego wg IB DP Biology guide (first assessment 2025), oznaczone „IB …”

items.question: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration?
items.explanation: Most of the ATP in a eukaryotic cell is produced in the mitochondria.

items.question: Which structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?
Which organelles are the site of protein synthesis?
What type of cell has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles?
items.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes; their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm.

items.question: How many micrometres are there in one millimetre?

items.text: Water moves across a partially permeable membrane by {{osmosis}}.
items.explanation: Water moves from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one.

items.text: The net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration is called {{diffusion}}.
Moving substances against a concentration gradient using energy from ATP is called {{active transport}}.
Plant cell walls are made mainly of {{cellulose}}.
Mitosis produces two {{genetically identical}} daughter nuclei.
items.explanation: Mitosis is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

items.question: What are the monomers of proteins?
Which bond links amino acids in a polypeptide?
items.explanation: It forms in a condensation reaction that releases water.

items.question: What is the region of an enzyme where the substrate binds called?
Which molecule is the main energy currency of the cell?
Which reagent turns blue-black in the presence of starch?
What are the products of aerobic respiration?

items.text: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the {{activation energy}}.
At high temperatures an enzyme {{denatures}} and its active site changes shape.
items.explanation: The substrate no longer fits, so the rate of reaction falls.

items.text: Glucose and fructose are examples of {{monosaccharides / monosaccharide}}.
Anaerobic respiration in human muscles produces {{lactate / lactic acid}}.

items.question: What is the shape of a DNA molecule?
Which base pairs with adenine in DNA?
Which base replaces thymine in RNA?
How many chromosomes are in a normal human body cell?
What term describes an organism with two different alleles of a gene?
What is a random change in the base sequence of DNA called?

items.text: Different versions of the same gene are called {{alleles / allele}}.
Meiosis produces {{haploid}} gametes with half the number of chromosomes.
Charles Darwin proposed evolution by {{natural selection}}.

items.question: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
Which chamber of the heart pumps blood to the rest of the body?
items.explanation: It has the thickest muscular wall of the four chambers.

items.question: Which hormone lowers blood glucose concentration?
Which organ produces insulin?
Which white blood cells produce antibodies?

items.text: Gas exchange in the lungs takes place in the {{alveoli / alveolus}}.
Red blood cells contain {{haemoglobin / hemoglobin}}, which binds oxygen.
Most digested food is absorbed in the {{small intestine / ileum}}.

items.question: Which pigment absorbs light for photosynthesis?
Through which pores in leaves does gas exchange occur?
Which tissue transports water from the roots to the leaves?
Which tissue transports sugars around a plant?
items.explanation: This movement of sugars is called translocation.

items.question: Which gas is released as a by-product of photosynthesis?

items.text: Photosynthesis takes place in the {{chloroplasts / chloroplast}}.
The loss of water vapour from leaves is called {{transpiration}}.

items.question: What is an organism that makes its own food called?
Roughly what percentage of energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
items.explanation: The rest is lost mainly as heat from respiration.

items.question: What is the role and position of a species in its ecosystem called?
Which gas released by burning fossil fuels is the main contributor to the greenhouse effect?

items.text: Producers are eaten by {{primary consumers}}.
All the populations of different species living in one area form a {{community}}.
Organisms that break down dead material are called {{decomposers / saprotrophs}}.

items.question: What is the variable you deliberately change in an experiment called?
What is the variable you measure in an experiment called?
Which statistic shows how spread out data are around the mean?

items.text: Variables kept the same throughout an experiment are called {{control variables / controlled variables}}.
Repeating trials and calculating a mean improves the {{reliability}} of the results.
The main biogenic elements are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and {{sulfur / sulphur}}.
items.explanation: These six macroelements build almost all organic molecules of the cell.

items.question: Which element is found in all proteins but not in carbohydrates or simple lipids?
items.explanation: Every amino acid contains an amino group (-NH2).

items.question: Which microelement is a component of haemoglobin and is needed to transport oxygen?
items.explanation: Iron deficiency leads to anaemia.

items.question: Which microelement is needed to make thyroid hormones such as thyroxine?
items.explanation: Iodine deficiency causes goitre (enlarged thyroid).

items.question: Which microelement strengthens tooth enamel and bones?
items.explanation: Fluoride is added to toothpaste to prevent tooth decay.

items.text: Water is an excellent {{solvent}} because its molecules are polar.
items.explanation: Ions and polar molecules dissolve in water, so it is the medium of all metabolic reactions.

items.question: What type of bond forms between neighbouring water molecules?
items.explanation: Hydrogen bonds explain the cohesion, high boiling point and high heat capacity of water.

items.text: Because of its high {{specific heat capacity}}, water warms up and cools down slowly, which stabilises body temperature.
items.hint: a lot of energy is needed to raise its temperature

items.question: What is the attraction between water molecules that lets water move up narrow xylem vessels called?
items.explanation: Cohesion (water to water) and adhesion (water to the vessel wall) together cause capillary action.

items.question: Which two monosaccharides make up sucrose?
items.explanation: Sucrose is the sugar transported in plants and used as table sugar.

items.question: Which polysaccharide is the storage carbohydrate of animals, found in liver and muscle?
items.explanation: Plants store glucose as starch, animals as glycogen.

items.question: Which pentose sugar is found in RNA nucleotides?
items.explanation: DNA contains deoxyribose, which has one oxygen atom fewer.

items.text: A protein that contains a non-protein part, such as the haem group in haemoglobin, is a {{complex / conjugated}} protein.
items.explanation: Simple proteins consist only of amino acids.

items.question: Which fibrous structural protein is the main component of tendons, skin and bone?
items.explanation: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body.

items.question: Which protein builds hair, nails and the outer layer of the skin?

items.text: A simple lipid (triglyceride) consists of one molecule of {{glycerol}} and three fatty acids.
items.explanation: Fats and oils are triglycerides; they are insoluble in water and store energy.

items.question: Which complex lipids are the main building blocks of cell membranes?
items.explanation: A phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty-acid tails.

items.question: Which sugar is found in DNA nucleotides?
Name the three components of a nucleotide.
accept: phosphate group, pentose sugar, nitrogenous base
items.explanation: In DNA the sugar is deoxyribose; in RNA it is ribose.

items.question: Which structure inside the nucleus produces ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits?
What is the double membrane surrounding the nucleus called?
items.explanation: Its pores allow mRNA to leave the nucleus and proteins to enter.

items.question: Which organelle modifies, packages and sorts proteins for secretion?
Which organelles contain digestive enzymes that break down worn-out cell parts and engulfed material?

items.text: The {{rough endoplasmic reticulum / rough ER}} is studded with ribosomes and synthesises proteins for export from the cell.
items.hint: membrane system continuous with the nuclear envelope

items.question: Which large fluid-filled organelle stores water and keeps a plant cell turgid?
items.explanation: The vacuole is surrounded by a membrane called the tonoplast.

items.text: Fungal cell walls are made of {{chitin}}, whereas plant cell walls are made of cellulose.
items.hint: the same polysaccharide as in insect exoskeletons

items.question: In a prokaryotic cell, what is the region containing the circular DNA molecule called?
items.explanation: The nucleoid is not surrounded by a membrane.

items.text: The theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral cell is the {{endosymbiotic}} theory.
items.explanation: Evidence: both organelles have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and a double membrane.

items.question: Which network of protein fibres gives a cell its shape and moves organelles and chromosomes?
items.explanation: It consists of microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments.

items.text: The cell membrane is a {{phospholipid}} bilayer with embedded proteins.
items.explanation: The fluid mosaic model: lipids and proteins can move within the layer.

items.question: What type of transport moves glucose across a membrane down its concentration gradient through a carrier protein, without using ATP?
items.explanation: Simple diffusion needs no protein; active transport needs a protein and ATP.

items.question: What is the process by which a cell takes in large particles or fluid by enclosing them in a vesicle?
items.explanation: Phagocytosis (solids) and pinocytosis (liquids) are types of endocytosis.

items.text: Releasing substances from a cell in vesicles that fuse with the cell membrane is called {{exocytosis}}.
items.explanation: Hormones and digestive enzymes leave cells by exocytosis.

items.text: An animal cell placed in a {{hypotonic}} solution takes in water by osmosis and may burst.
items.hint: the solution is more dilute than the cytoplasm
items.explanation: A plant cell in the same solution becomes turgid thanks to its wall.

items.text: In a hypertonic solution a plant cell loses water and its protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall; this is {{plasmolysis}}.
items.explanation: Plasmolysis can be observed in onion epidermis placed in concentrated salt solution.

items.question: How do you calculate the total magnification of a light microscope?
items.explanation: E.g. 10x eyepiece and 40x objective give 400x.

items.question: What thin glass plate is placed over a specimen on a microscope slide?
items.explanation: Lower it at an angle to avoid trapping air bubbles.

items.question: Which objective lens should you use first when focusing a microscope?
items.explanation: Find and centre the specimen at low power before switching to a higher power.

items.question: What is the formula for the magnification of a drawing or photograph?
accept: image size divided by actual size
items.explanation: Rearranged: actual size = image size / magnification.

items.text: Enzymes are biological catalysts, and almost all of them are {{proteins}}.
items.explanation: Their 3D shape, including the active site, depends on the amino acid sequence.

items.question: What term describes the fact that an enzyme acts on only one substrate or one type of reaction?
items.explanation: The substrate fits the active site like a key fits a lock.

items.question: Which enzyme breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen?
items.explanation: Catalase activity can be tested with liver or potato pieces in hydrogen peroxide.

items.text: Below the optimum temperature the rate of an enzyme reaction falls because molecules have less {{kinetic energy}} and collide less often.
items.explanation: Unlike heat denaturation, this effect is reversible.

items.question: What is the general term for all the chemical reactions taking place in a cell?

items.text: Reactions that build complex molecules from simpler ones and require energy are {{anabolic}} reactions.
items.explanation: Catabolic reactions break molecules down and release energy that drives anabolism.

items.question: What are the products of ATP hydrolysis?
items.explanation: Breaking the terminal phosphate bond releases energy used by the cell.

items.question: What are the substrates of aerobic respiration?
items.explanation: Products: carbon dioxide, water and energy stored in ATP.

items.question: Under what condition do human muscle cells switch to lactic acid fermentation?
items.explanation: During intense exercise oxygen supply is too low for aerobic respiration alone.

items.question: How many ATP molecules are gained from one glucose molecule in lactic acid fermentation?
items.explanation: Aerobic respiration yields about 30 ATP per glucose, roughly fifteen times more.

items.question: What is the breakdown of glycogen into glucose called?
items.explanation: It supplies glucose from liver and muscle stores when energy demand rises.

items.text: Word equation of photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water -> {{glucose}} + oxygen (light and chlorophyll needed).

items.question: In which part of the chloroplast does the Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions) take place?
items.explanation: The light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes.

items.text: In the nucleus, DNA is wound around proteins called {{histones}}, forming chromatin.
items.explanation: Before division chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes.

items.question: What is a cell with two sets of chromosomes (2n) called?
items.explanation: Human body cells are diploid (46); gametes are haploid (23).

items.question: In which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
items.explanation: After S phase the amount of DNA in the nucleus is doubled.

items.text: The longest part of the cell cycle, between two divisions, is {{interphase}}.
items.explanation: Interphase consists of G1, S and G2 phases.

items.question: What term describes DNA replication, in which each new molecule keeps one original strand?
items.explanation: Each strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand.

items.question: Name the four phases of mitosis in order.
items.explanation: Prophase: chromosomes condense; metaphase: line up; anaphase: separate; telophase: nuclei re-form.

items.question: What is the division of the cytoplasm that follows nuclear division called?
How many daughter cells result from one cell undergoing meiosis?
items.explanation: Meiosis consists of two consecutive divisions.

items.text: In humans, meiosis takes place only in the gonads, producing {{gametes}} (sperm and egg cells).
items.explanation: Mitosis serves growth and tissue repair; meiosis serves sexual reproduction.

items.question: What is programmed cell death, e.g. removal of the tissue between fingers in an embryo, called?
items.explanation: Apoptosis also removes damaged or infected cells.

items.question: What is a testable statement that predicts the outcome of an experiment called?
items.explanation: A hypothesis is accepted or rejected on the basis of the results.

items.text: The sample treated exactly like the experimental one except for the tested factor is the {{control}} group.
items.explanation: Without a control you cannot tell whether the tested factor caused the effect.

items.question: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix during replication?
items.explanation: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.

items.question: Which enzyme adds complementary nucleotides to the growing DNA strand during replication?

items.text: {{Transcription}} is the synthesis of mRNA from a DNA template by RNA polymerase.
items.explanation: It takes place in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells.

items.question: What is the synthesis of a polypeptide on a ribosome, using the sequence of mRNA, called?
How many mRNA bases make up one codon?
items.explanation: Each codon specifies one amino acid or a stop signal.

items.question: Which type of RNA carries amino acids to the ribosome?
items.explanation: The tRNA anticodon pairs with the complementary codon on mRNA.

items.question: What is the maintenance of a stable internal environment, e.g. constant body temperature, called?
items.explanation: Thermoregulation, osmoregulation and blood pressure control are examples.

items.question: What type of feedback mechanism maintains homeostasis by reversing a change?
items.explanation: E.g. a rise in blood glucose triggers insulin, which lowers it again.

items.question: In the binomial name Homo sapiens, which word is the genus?
items.explanation: The second word (sapiens) is the species epithet; the whole name is written in italics.

items.question: Which taxonomic rank is directly above species?
items.explanation: Order of ranks: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.text: The three domains of life are Bacteria, Archaea and {{Eukarya / Eukaryota / Eukaryotes}}.
items.explanation: Only Eukarya have cells with a nucleus.

items.question: What is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring called?
